text:
The Long Way Home

On the evening of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. James Lovell, the commander, was a veteran of three earlier flights and was making his fourth trip into space. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was on his first. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles, and flight surgeons grounded him. Swigert had trained for the role as a backup, and he stepped in with little time to spare.

The first two days were almost dull, and that was a good sign. The crew nicknamed their command module Odyssey and their lunar lander Aquarius. They pulled the lander free of its rocket stage, checked their systems and settled into the routine of a long coast. On the evening of April 13 they finished a television broadcast that few networks bothered to carry, showing viewers around the cabin and saying goodnight. Millions of people had come to treat Moon flights as ordinary business. Within minutes that view would change.

About fifty five hours into the flight, and roughly two hundred thousand miles from home, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the oxygen tanks in the service module. Stirring kept the supercold liquid oxygen from settling in layers and gave the gauges a true reading. Swigert flipped the switch. A few moments later the men heard a bang and felt the spacecraft shudder. Warning lights lit up, and the voltage on the electrical buses began to sag. Swigert reported the trouble to Houston, and Lovell repeated it. The words that became famous were, "Houston, we've had a problem."

The cause lay in a chain of small errors that began years earlier. The second oxygen tank had been dropped slightly during assembly, and it was later damaged in a ground test. When technicians drained it before launch, they used a heater that was never meant to run at the higher voltage the ground power supplied. The heater's thermostat switches welded shut, and the wiring insulation was baked without anyone noticing. When Swigert threw the stirring switch, a spark ignited that damaged insulation inside a tank full of pure oxygen. The pressure rose until the tank burst and tore a panel off the side of the service module. The second tank was crippled, and the first soon leaked away as well.

Oxygen mattered for two reasons. The crew needed it to breathe, but the fuel cells that made the spacecraft's electricity also consumed it. Without oxygen the command module would lose power, water and the means to survive reentry. Lovell looked out a window and saw gas streaming into space, and he understood the Moon was no longer the goal. The only question was whether the three of them could get back.

Flight director Gene Kranz and his teams on the ground worked through the night. The crew first tried to save the command module, but power kept draining, and within hours they had to shut it down to preserve what battery life remained. The answer was already attached to the ship. The lunar module Aquarius had its own oxygen, water, batteries and engine. It was built to carry two men for about two days on the Moon, and now it had to carry three men for four days. The crew crawled into the lander and used it as a lifeboat.

The trajectory raised another problem. Apollo 13 had been aimed to pass behind the Moon on a path that could swing it home, but an earlier course change meant the ship was no longer on that safe route. Controllers first used the lander's descent engine to put it back on a path that would carry the ship around the Moon and toward Earth. Later, after the ship had looped behind the Moon, they ordered a second burn to speed the return and bring the landing area closer in time. On the far side of the Moon the crew passed farther from Earth than any humans before or since, nearly two hundred fifty thousand miles away. Lovell later said he hardly had time to enjoy the view.

Staying alive was the next test. Aquarius had no way to filter that many breaths. Carbon dioxide began to build in the cabin, and the lander's filters could not keep up. The command module had plenty of filters, but they were square, and the lander's sockets were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the same items the crew had aboard, including plastic bags, cardboard, a spacesuit hose and duct tape. They built an adapter and read the instructions to the crew by radio. The crew copied it, and the carbon dioxide level fell to safe numbers.

Conditions grew harsh. The crew shut down almost everything to save power, and the cabin temperature dropped close to freezing. Condensation beaded on the walls. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a fever and a painful infection. The men slept little and ate cold food. They watched a failing, cooling spacecraft through windows that fogged over, while the Earth they needed to reach looked small and far away.

Meanwhile, Ken Mattingly, the grounded pilot, worked in a simulator on the ground. The command module had to be brought back to life before reentry, and it had to be done with very little power. Mattingly and the engineers worked out a startup sequence that kept the draw within the limits of the batteries. Their procedure was read up to the crew near the end, and it worked.

One last course correction remained. The ship was drifting, and its angle of entry into the atmosphere had to be right. Too shallow, and the capsule would bounce off into space. Too steep, and it would burn up. With the guidance system off, the crew used the lit edge of the Earth as a visual reference and fired the lander's engine by hand for about fourteen seconds.

On April 17, the crew separated from the service module and finally saw the damage. A whole side panel was gone, and the exposed equipment was scorched and twisted. Haise and Lovell then moved to Odyssey, and they released Aquarius, which had saved their lives and would burn up in the atmosphere. Reentry brought a long radio blackout. It was supposed to last about three minutes, but it ran longer, and in Houston the room fell quiet as the clock ticked past the expected time. Then the radio crackled, and Swigert's voice came through.

Odyssey's parachutes opened, and the capsule dropped into the South Pacific near Samoa. A recovery ship, the Iwo Jima, picked the crew up within minutes. They had been gone nearly six days. All three were tired, thin and dehydrated, but they were alive.

Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, yet many people count it among the finest hours of the space program. A failure became a rescue because thousands of people refused to treat the situation as hopeless. The investigation that followed changed the design of the oxygen tanks and the wiring around them, and later Apollo crews landed on the Moon with a safer spacecraft. The crew returned home with a simple lesson. Fly the problem in front of you, and trust the people who are working beside you.
